repos.title: Deep Photo Style Transfer
repos.paper_summary: The paper introduces a deep-learning method for photographic style transfer that preserves the photorealism of the input image while accurately matching the color and texture of a reference style image. The approach extends the Neural Style algorithm by adding two constraints to the optimization objective. First, a photorealism regularization term ensures the transformation from input to output is locally affine in color space, preventing spatial distortions like wiggly edges. This term uses the Matting Laplacian matrix derived from the input image. Second, an augmented style loss incorporates semantic segmentation masks for both images, restricting style transfer between semantically equivalent regions (e.g., sky to sky) to prevent "spillover" artifacts. The method uses a pre-trained VGG-19 network, with content features from `conv4_2` and style features from layers `conv1_1` through `conv5_1`. Optimization runs in 3–5 minutes on an NVIDIA Titan X GPU. In user studies, the method produced photorealistic results comparable to global histogram transfer methods, but achieved higher style faithfulness than Reinhard et al., Pitié et al., and Photoshop Match Color in over 80% of comparisons. Limitations include failure cases under extreme semantic mismatch between input and reference, which require manual segmentation masks to resolve.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Photographic style transfer must avoid painting-like distortion while keeping the reference style faithful.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: The method adds a locally affine color regularizer and semantic segmentation masks to Neural Style optimization.

digest_headlines.heading: Implementation Details
digest_headlines.headline: The implementation uses a pretrained convolutional network, two-stage optimization and merged segmentation classes.

digest_headlines.heading: Results and Comparison
digest_headlines.headline: Compared with Neural Style, patch-based and global transfer methods, the approach avoids distortion and was judged most faithful more than 80% of the time.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: The approach transfers reference style faithfully across time of day, weather, season and artistic edits while keeping outputs photorealistic.

repos.title: Watch Your Step: Anticipated Perception for Humanoid Locomotion
repos.paper_summary: Watch Your Step introduces a perceptive locomotion framework for the Unitree G1 humanoid in which a lightweight foothold prediction model (FPM) predicts the next two footholds from proprioception and the velocity command, and the policy observes only small 7×7 elevation-map patches around those predicted footholds. The FPM is an MLP with two 128-unit hidden layers, trained by Huber regression on labeled footholds from recent policy rollouts and refit every 500 PPO iterations, jointly with a PPO locomotion policy. On the training terrain curriculum, the FPM policy reaches level 5 after 7.5k iterations, against 26.1k for the complete-map baseline (HM) and 20.0k for an attention-based encoder (AME2). AME2 ends slightly higher at 40k iterations but needs four GPUs and 6.3 s per policy update versus 0.55 s. In simulation, the FPM policy achieves 74.2% success on sparse corridor terrain versus 71.7% for AME2 and at most 42.7% for the other baselines, and 77.7% on out-of-distribution gaps. The policy transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 on stairs, a 0.55 m gap, and a 0.6 m drop. Limitations include reliance on an elevation map and that the policy's cautious behavior near unseen gaps is a hypothesis rather than a measured result.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Predicting footholds from proprioception and filtering the elevation map around them should cut redundant input for perceptive humanoid locomotion.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: The locomotion task is set as a reinforcement learning problem for a 29-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid trained with PPO in 8192 parallel environments.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A blind foothold predictor is retrained periodically, and the policy sees only small height patches around its two predicted footholds.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments and Results
digest_headlines.headline: The gated policy reaches curriculum level 5 in 7.5k iterations, 3.4 to 3.5 times faster than full-map methods.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: The approach trails full-map methods on stepped corridor terrain and cannot see obstacles approaching from the side.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Sampling the elevation map around predicted footholds learns faster than full-map policies and transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1.

repos.title: ChatDev: Communicative Agents for Software Development
repos.paper_summary:
ChatDev is a multi-agent software development framework that uses LLM-driven agents to execute design, coding, and testing phases through structured dialogue. The system organizes work via a "chat chain," which breaks tasks into subtasks handled by pairs of agents acting as instructor and assistant. A "communicative dehallucination" mechanism reduces errors by having the assistant request specific details before generating code.

Evaluated on a dataset of 1,200 software requirements, ChatDev outperforms GPT-Engineer and MetaGPT. In Table 1, ChatDev achieves an executability score of 0.880 and a quality score of 0.395, compared to 0.415 and 0.152 for MetaGPT. Pairwise evaluations in Table 2 show ChatDev winning 77.1% of comparisons against GPT-Engineer when judged by GPT-4. Ablations in Table 4 indicate that removing agent roles drops executability from 0.880 to 0.580. Limitations include high computational costs due to multiple agents and a tendency to generate simple logic or static placeholders rather than complex database interactions, making it suitable primarily for prototypes.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: ChatDev uses chat among role-playing LLM agents, with language as the shared medium, across design, coding, and testing.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work covers LLM agents and deep learning applied to single waterfall phases, which the authors say remain isolated.

digest_headlines.heading: ChatDev
digest_headlines.headline: ChatDev pairs an instructor agent and an assistant agent per subtask, linked by a chat chain and dehallucination rules.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: ChatDev scores highest on all four metrics and wins most pairwise comparisons against GPT-Engineer and MetaGPT.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Authors conclude that language-based multi-agent communication improves software optimization and supports agent autonomy.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Agents need detailed requirements, evaluation covers limited dimensions, and multi-agent runs need more tokens and time.

repos.title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
repos.paper_summary: SWE-bench is an evaluation benchmark of 2294 software engineering tasks drawn from GitHub issues and their merged pull requests across 12 popular Python repositories. A model receives an issue text and a codebase snapshot and must produce a patch that makes the repository's fail-to-pass tests pass without breaking existing tests. Tasks were collected with a 33-stage pipeline that filters PRs for issue resolution, test changes, and successful execution. The authors also release SWE-bench Lite, a 300-instance subset, a training set (SWE-bench-train, about 19,000 instances from 37 other repositories), and two fine-tuned CodeLlama-Python models, SWE-Llama 7b and 13b, trained with LoRA on attention weights. Context is selected with BM25 retrieval or with oracle files from the reference patch. The best model, Claude 2 with BM25 retrieval, resolves 1.96% of tasks; with oracle retrieval it resolves 4.8%. Performance falls as context length grows. The authors note that the benchmark covers only Python, and that execution-based tests do not capture code efficiency, readability, or comprehensiveness.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing benchmarks are saturated, so the authors propose SWE-bench, which draws tasks from real GitHub issues.

digest_headlines.heading: SWE-bench
digest_headlines.headline: SWE-bench pairs GitHub issues with merged pull requests and grades patches by running the repository's tests.

digest_headlines.heading: SWE-Llama: Fine-tuning CodeLlama for SWE-bench
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-tuning CodeLlama-Python on issue-patch pairs produces SWE-Llama, open models that edit repositories.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Each model gets context from sparse retrieval or from oracle files that the reference patch edits.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Claude 2 is the best model at 1.96% resolved, and resolution falls as the total context length grows.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier benchmarks use narrow tasks or single functions, which SWE-bench extends to multi-file repository edits.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Limitations include Python-only tasks, simple baselines, and execution tests that miss readability and efficiency.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics Statement
digest_headlines.headline: SWE-bench uses public repositories with licenses permitting software use, and involves no human subjects or GitHub user data.

digest_headlines.heading: Reproducibility Statement
digest_headlines.headline: The source code, all 2294 task instances, and technical details for collection and evaluation are provided for reproduction.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers construction, field definitions, execution-based validation, dataset statistics, and case studies of model patches.

repos.title: Co-Design Bench: Multimodal Collaborative Coding Evaluation for Agentic Models
repos.paper_summary: Co-Design Bench is a reference-free benchmark for coding agents that revise real users' web applications from multimodal requests. It contains 273 tasks drawn from 37,463 deduplicated queries across 26,314 real coding sessions, split into Multimodal Editing (100 tasks, optional image, audio, video, or document inputs) and Repository Editing (173 tasks, coordinated multi-file changes). Each task has a runnable pre-edit app and hidden expert-authored acceptance criteria (2,331 in total). Grading is a "judge-then-refute" protocol: a fixed LLM evaluator assigns Pass, Partial, or Fail per criterion from source diffs, renders, and browser traces, then a separate LLM verifier challenges positive verdicts. Under a shared Claude Code harness, the strongest of ten endpoints (gpt-6-astra) reaches a mean strict criterion completion of 0.699 but fully completes only 26.4% of tasks. All ten endpoints score lower on repository edits spanning three or four change types than on those spanning one or two. A limitation is that tasks evaluate a fixed request without simulated user feedback.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Co-Design Bench tests whether coding agents turn real users' multimodal revision requests into working application changes.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior benchmarks cover screenshot reconstruction, predefined edits, and repository issues, but few cover compound revisions drawn from real coding sessions.

digest_headlines.heading: Co-Design Bench
digest_headlines.headline: Each task pairs a runnable pre-edit application with a normalized request, attachments, and hidden expert-authored criteria.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation Protocol
digest_headlines.headline: A judge grades each criterion from source and browser evidence, then a separate verifier challenges positive verdicts.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Across ten endpoints, criterion coverage runs well ahead of complete delivery, with the top model fully passing 26.4% of tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Co-Design Bench offers a shared setting for measuring complete delivery, with runnable baselines and criterion-level evidence retained.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the WebCompass execution-regime comparison, evaluator sensitivity, resource accounting, cases, dataset composition, and evaluation details.

repos.title: Step-DPO: Step-wise Preference Optimization for Long-chain Reasoning of LLMs
repos.paper_summary:
Step-DPO is a preference optimization method for large language models that treats individual reasoning steps, rather than full answers, as the unit of comparison to improve mathematical reasoning. The method modifies the standard Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) objective by conditioning on preceding correct steps and optimizing the probability of the next correct step versus the first erroneous step. This allows the model to pinpoint specific errors in long chains of thought without penalizing earlier correct logic.

The authors construct a dataset of 10K preference pairs using a three-step pipeline: collecting incorrect model outputs, localizing the first error, and sampling self-generated corrections from the reference model. They find that using in-distribution data generated by the model itself yields better results than out-of-distribution data written by humans or GPT-4. On the MATH benchmark, applying Step-DPO to Qwen2-72B-Instruct increases accuracy from 69.4% to 70.8%, while GSM8K accuracy rises from 92.4% to 94.0%. These gains are achieved with fewer than 500 training steps. The approach also improves performance on competition-level problems like AIME 2024, where Qwen2-72B-Instruct scores 4/30 compared to 5/30 for the base instruct model.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Vanilla DPO cannot locate errors in long math reasoning, so Step-DPO compares individual reasoning steps instead.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Prior methods improve math reasoning through prompting, data augmentation or reinforcement learning, but each has stated limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Step-DPO
digest_headlines.headline: Step-DPO builds preference pairs from the first wrong step, with the model's own correct continuation as the preferred choice.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Step-DPO raises Qwen2-72B-Instruct to 70.8% on MATH, with approximately a 3% boost for models above 70B.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude Step-DPO with 10K pairs gives significant gains, particularly for large models.

repos.title: Agensh: Scaling Organizational Intelligence to 1,024 Agents
repos.paper_summary:
Agensh is a multi-agent harness that coordinates concurrent LLM workers without a central orchestrator. Each worker executes an asynchronous loop: gathering context, claiming sub-tasks, taking action, verifying results, and merging progress into a shared workspace. Coordination relies on three infrastructure components: a Git-based shared workspace for code integration, a message interface for peer communication, and a shared context board for reusable findings.

The paper evaluates Agensh on the five hardest ProgramBench tasks using GPT-5.6-sol (high) with a 6-hour budget. Scaling from 1 to 128 agents increases the mean final test-pass rate from 19.31% to 28.78%, a 49% relative improvement. On the pandoc task, scaling to 1,024 agents raises the final test-pass rate from 33.89% to 55.06%. Larger organizations also reach comparable performance levels earlier; for instance, 128 agents exceed a 30% pass rate at 30 minutes, while single agents remain below this threshold for two hours. Limitations include reliance on specific underlying models and harnesses, and the need for staggered agent activation to manage scope contention in large-scale deployments.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Agensh replaces a central orchestrator with self-organized workers, and scaling 1 to 128 agents raises mean test-pass rate from 19.31% to 28.78%.

digest_headlines.heading: Multi-Agent Organization Harness
digest_headlines.headline: Each worker repeats a five-step loop over a shared workspace, message interface and shared context, with no central orchestrator.

digest_headlines.heading: Scaling Multi-Agent Organization to 1,024 Agents
digest_headlines.headline: Mean test-pass rate rises with 8, 32 and 128 agents, and pandoc reaches 55.06% with 1,024 agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior harnesses keep task assignment under a fixed lead or trained orchestrator, while some tools coordinate workers through shared state.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Agent count is proposed as a new scaling dimension, though every reported run uses one agent model.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives the worker prompt, the event-driven runtime, the experiment configuration and the staggered agent launch schedule.

repos.title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
repos.paper_summary: OpenVLHarness is a multimodal tool-use harness for MLLMs, built around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer wraps heterogeneous perception, search, and computation tools behind task-level interfaces and renders their outputs into model-readable observations. Memory registers images, structured data, and web references under handles, and a Python Coding Agent runs generated programs over stored values, so later steps can reuse earlier evidence. The harness is evaluated on 22 benchmarks across four domains with eight backbones. Averaged over the 22 datasets, it raises Qwen3-VL-8B from 34.2 to 45.4 and Qwen3-VL-32B from 38.3 to 50.9, outperforming OctoTools and Visual Sketchpad. With GPT-6 Luna at medium effort, it scores 56.5 against 45.8 for the base model, and it is reported to outperform Codex and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort while using at most 37% of their model-token cost. Qwen3-VL results are means of three seeds; GPT-6 results are single runs, so their variance is unreported in the main table. The paper's benchmark-level gains are uneven, with some datasets, such as V* for Qwen3-VL-8B, showing no gain.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Extra reasoning budget gives diminishing returns, so the paper proposes OpenVLHarness to add multimodal evidence acquisition.

digest_headlines.heading: Harness Design
digest_headlines.headline: OpenVLHarness pairs a capability layer that renders tool outputs with persistent memory of handle-addressed artifacts.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: OpenVLHarness raises Qwen3-VL-8B scores on 22 benchmarks, for example from 32.00 to 48.56 on a counting benchmark.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior visual tool-use systems use fixed plans or task-specific frameworks, while this paper keeps multimodal artifacts addressable across turns.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Released harness gives broad gains on 22 benchmarks and can specialize to domains without updating model weights.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix reports tool-call volume, capability distribution, paired accuracy effects, and object-count distributions of benchmarks.

repos.title: SubRoformer: Subband Time-Domain Representation for Music Source Separation
repos.paper_summary: SubRoFormer is a Transformer-based music source separation system that splits a stereo mix into frequency-localized subbands, runs a separator on temporally compressed features, and predicts complex masks at 100 Hz. The subband module uses an overlapping triangular FIR filter bank, complex analytic conversion, baseband demodulation, and decimation, with a fast polyphase implementation. The separator combines a patched axial RoFormer (alternating subband-axis and temporal-axis attention with rotary embeddings) with a GEGLU gated residual fusion that merges coarse and fine-rate features. On MUSDB18-HQ, training only on that dataset, the target-specific models reach an average SDR of 10.63 dB across four stems, 0.61 dB above the strongest complete public-data BS-RoFormer result the authors report, and 0.99 dB above the reported Mel-RoFormer result. BS-RoFormer is 1.38 dB better on bass. With 500 extra training songs, a single multi-stem model reaches 11.59 dB. The subband transform alone reconstructs the mixture at 27.8 dB SDR-scale fidelity for mel and ERB banks, far below the near-perfect STFT and MDCT controls. The authors state the results are single-seed and directional, and that repeated seeds, efficiency measurements, and parameter-matched ablations are still needed.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Subband frontend plus a residual RoFormer separator targets the time-frequency trade-off in music source separation.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior systems span waveform, hybrid, spectrogram, and subband separators, and the paper positions itself among them.

digest_headlines.heading: Subband Time-Domain Representation
digest_headlines.headline: A fixed triangular subband filter bank with polyphase implementation reconstructs the mixture with measured distortion.

digest_headlines.heading: Residual SubRoFormer
digest_headlines.headline: SubRoFormer combines fine-rate features, a patched axial RoFormer, and gated residual fusion to predict complex masks.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments use MUSDB18-HQ with SDR as the primary metric, and training data and augmentation are described.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: SubRoFormer-B reaches 10.63 dB on MUSDB18-HQ without extra data, but the authors call the evidence preliminary.

repos.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
repos.paper_summary: The Switch Transformer replaces the standard feed-forward layer in Transformers with a sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) module that routes each token to a single expert, reducing communication overhead and improving training stability. By using top-1 routing instead of top-k, the model maintains constant computational cost per token while scaling parameter count. The paper introduces selective precision casting to stabilize bfloat16 training and an auxiliary load-balancing loss to ensure uniform expert usage. Experiments on the C4 corpus show that a 64-expert Switch-Base model achieves the same pre-training quality as T5-Base in one-seventh the time. Fine-tuning results indicate consistent improvements over T5-Base and T5-Large on GLUE, SuperGLUE, SQuAD, and summarization tasks. Distilling these sparse models into dense T5-Base architectures preserves approximately 30% of the quality gain while compressing model size by up to 99%. In multilingual settings across 101 languages, the method yields a mean 5x speedup over mT5-Base. A limitation is that distillation does not fully recover teacher performance, and the approach relies on specific hardware parallelism strategies for trillion-parameter scales.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse expert routing is proposed to add parameters without raising per-example compute, with gains across pre-training, fine-tuning and multilingual training.

digest_headlines.heading: Switch Transformer
digest_headlines.headline: Routing each token to one expert simplifies Mixture of Experts, with capacity limits and a balancing loss keeping training stable.

digest_headlines.heading: Scaling Properties
digest_headlines.headline: Increasing experts at fixed FLOPS per token speeds up pre-training, with Switch-Base 64 reaching T5-Base quality in one-seventh the time.

digest_headlines.heading: Downstream Results
digest_headlines.headline: Switch models improve most T5 fine-tuning tasks, distill to dense models keeping 30% of gains, and beat mT5 on all 101 languages.

digest_headlines.heading: Designing Models with Data, Model, and Expert-Parallelism
digest_headlines.headline: Data, model and expert parallelism combine to train 395 billion and 1.6 trillion parameter Switch models, with Switch-XXL sometimes unstable.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work scales models through model parallelism and conditional computation, including mixture of experts and attention sparsity.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse models are argued to outperform dense models per step and on wall clock time, but distilled versions keep only about 30% of gains.

digest_headlines.heading: Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Remaining challenges include stabilizing the largest models, heterogeneous experts, expert layers beyond feed-forward layers, and other modalities.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Switch Transformers are presented as stable, sample-efficient language learners across pre-training, fine-tuning and multi-task training.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers attention Switch layers, token rerouting, router exploration, small-scale results, upstream-downstream correlation and pseudocode.
